Hooks: actions that run every time

Anything you write in a prompt or in CLAUDE.md is guidance. The model reads it and usually follows it, but it decides each time. A hook is not up to the model. It is a shell command that Claude Code runs whenever a particular event fires, whatever the model has decided. Use a hook when a rule must hold every single time: formatting after every edit, a lint before a turn can end, or a destructive command that must never run.
A hook has three parts. The
event
says when it fires. The
matcher
narrows it to particular tools, for example
or
. The
handler
is the command that runs. The event matters most, because it decides what the hook is able to do:
Commonly used hook events and what each one can do
Event
When it fires
Typical use
PreToolUse
Before a tool call executes; can block it
Deny a dangerous Bash command or an edit to a protected file
PostToolUse
After a tool call succeeds
Run a formatter on the file Claude just edited
Stop
When Claude finishes responding
Block the turn from ending until a check passes
SessionStart
When a session begins or resumes
Re-inject reminders, for example after compaction
Notification
When Claude Code sends a notification
Show a desktop alert when Claude needs your attention
Setup
On --init-only, or --init or --maintenance in -p mode
One-time preparation in CI or scripts

Skills and MCP servers as shared team tooling
Every developer's session starts from the same checked-in files.
CLAUDE.md as implementation guidance

holds the project's conventions. Next to it, hooks enforce rules and Skills package repeatable procedures. Together these three put the whole team on the same workflow without anyone having to configure it locally.
Agent Skills (SKILL.md)
are reusable prompt packages. Checked into the repo, they become a team prompt library. A developer runs a procedure like the one below as
, and every teammate's run follows the same eight steps: read the issue, fix it, test, lint, commit and open a PR.
A repo-level skill that turns the issue-fixing procedure into one command
markdown

MCP servers are how Claude reaches external systems. When a team wants Claude to query its PostgreSQL database during a session, the fitting approach is to configure an MCP server for that database. The server exposes tools, Claude discovers them through the protocol, and the team writes no tool-execution code of its own. The other options each fail in a specific way. A PreToolUse hook reacts to tool calls that are already happening but gives Claude no new tool. Unrestricted Bash access goes against the practice of permitting only specific tools you know are safe. A subagent whose prompt contains the schema knows about the database but has no way to query it.
Agent SDK query that connects a Postgres MCP server and allows only its read-only SQL tool

Exam trap
To let Claude query a database, write a hook that runs SQL whenever Claude asks for data.
Why is that wrong?

A subagent whose prompt includes the full database schema

Exam question

A team wants Claude Code to query their internal PostgreSQL database directly during a session, without the team writing custom tool-execution code themselves. Which approach fits the Model Context Protocol integration model?
Configure an MCP server for the database and let Claude discover its tools through the protocol
Write a PreToolUse hook that executes SQL queries whenever Claude requests database access
Grant the Bash tool unrestricted access so Claude can invoke the database's command-line client directly
Create a subagent whose system prompt contains the database schema and query examples

Running Claude Code in scripts and CI
Claude Code does not need someone at the keyboard. With
you pass a prompt, get the result on standard output, and can pipe data in, as in
. Any shell script, cron job or CI step can use it this way. The Setup hook event covers one-time preparation for these runs: it fires on
or
in
mode.
In GitHub, the Claude Code GitHub Action runs Claude in your CI pipeline. Running
from Claude Code installs the GitHub App, adds the authentication secret and opens a pull request with the workflow file. A workflow can run in one of two modes. With no
input, it waits for an
mention in an issue or PR and posts its progress as a comment. With a
input, Claude runs on the trigger alone, and its results go to the workflow run log unless the prompt tells it to post them.
The job portion of a mention-triggered workflow: permissions, checkout, then the action
yaml
The team's skill library carries over to CI. Put
before the Claude step so the files in
exist on the runner, then pass
as the prompt. Locally and in CI, the same skill runs the same procedure. To restrict tools in CI, pass flags through
, for example
naming the only tool the job may call.
Unattended runs have guardrails of their own. On issue and pull request events, the user who triggers a run must have write access to the repository. Bot actors are rejected unless they are listed in

, which stops bots from triggering Claude in a loop. For automation outside GitHub Actions, the Claude Agent SDK is the building block; the GitHub Action itself is built on it. If you only want reviews, Code Review gives every PR an automatic review without you writing a workflow.
